title: 1 Samuel 17:12–30
context: The narrator introduces David again as the youngest son of Jesse of Bethlehem, sent by his father with food for his brothers at the front. He hears Goliath’s challenge, asks what will be done for the man who removes the reproach from Israel, and calls Goliath one who defies the armies of the living God. His oldest brother Eliab rebukes him angrily. This section is part of a well-known textual question: a shorter Septuagint form of chapters 17–18, often listed from Codex Vaticanus, lacks 17:12–31, 17:41, 17:48b, 17:50, 17:55–18:5, 18:10–11, 18:17–19, and 18:29b–30. Some scholars think the Hebrew text has combined two accounts of David’s arrival; others think the Greek translator or its Hebrew source shortened the story to ease tensions with chapter 16. Neither view is settled, and both traditions read the canonical Hebrew account as a coherent narrative. They share the conviction that David’s zeal is for the honor of the living God.

verses.text: Now David was the son of that Ephrathite of Bethlehem Judah, whose name was Jesse; and he had eight sons. The man was an elderly old man in the days of Saul.
verses.arminianNotes:
David is introduced as the son of Jesse, an Ephrathite of Bethlehem in Judah who had eight sons and was elderly in Saul’s day. The reintroduction is one reason many readers see a separate strand here, and 1 Chronicles 2:13–15 lists seven sons, with David the seventh.

Arminian readers note that interpreters explain the difference variously, for instance by a son who died young, and that the narrative’s focus is David’s humble family origin.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the reintroduction of David after chapter 16 belongs to the textual and literary questions about this chapter, which scholars resolve in different ways without undermining its witness.

Both traditions see God choosing the youngest son of an ordinary family, consistent with his pattern of raising the lowly.

verses.text: The three oldest sons of Jesse had gone after Saul to the battle; and the names of his three sons who went to the battle were Eliab the firstborn, and next to him Abinadab, and the third Shammah.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jesse’s three oldest sons, Eliab, Abinadab and Shammah, have followed Saul to war. These are the brothers who passed before Samuel and were not chosen (16:6–10).

Arminian readers note that the brothers are serving honorably in the army, and that God’s choice of David did not make their faithful service worthless; each person remains responsible to serve where placed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the three brothers rejected at the anointing are now at the front, while the chosen one is still with the sheep, a reminder that God’s choice does not follow outward rank or appearance (16:7).

Both traditions see God’s choice of David as grace, not as a reward for status.

verses.text: David was the youngest; and the three oldest followed Saul.
verses.arminianNotes:
David is the youngest, and the three oldest follow Saul. The narrator underlines the contrast between the youngest son at home and the older brothers at war.

Arminian readers note that David’s place as youngest gave him humble work, and that his faithfulness in small tasks prepared him for larger ones, a pattern Jesus affirms in his teaching about faithfulness in little things (Luke 16:10).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that God’s purposes often run through the least likely member of a family, as with Jacob and Joseph, so that his choice is seen as free grace rather than natural right.

Both traditions read David’s youth as part of the story’s emphasis that God’s strength works through weakness.

verses.text: Now David went back and forth from Saul to feed his father’s sheep at Bethlehem.
verses.arminianNotes:
David goes back and forth between Saul and feeding his father’s sheep at Bethlehem. This verse seems to connect the account with David’s service at court in chapter 16.

Arminian readers note that David moves between royal service and humble shepherding without disdaining either, and that faithful ordinary work forms the character God uses.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that this verse may be the narrator’s way of linking David’s court service in chapter 16 with his presence at home here, and that interpreters weigh how the two accounts fit together.

Both traditions see David’s shepherding as training for the shepherd-king God intends him to be (compare 2 Samuel 5:2).

verses.text: The Philistine came near morning and evening, and presented himself forty days.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Philistine comes forward morning and evening for forty days. The repeated challenge prolongs Israel’s humiliation.

Arminian readers note that the long period of unanswered taunting shows how persistent fear can paralyze God’s people, and how much they need someone to respond in faith rather than wait for circumstances to change.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that forty is a number often associated in Scripture with testing, as in Israel’s forty years in the wilderness, though readers should not press the number into a code; God’s timing brings David at the appointed moment.

Both traditions read the forty days as deepening the crisis that God will resolve.

verses.text: Jesse said to David his son, “Now take for your brothers an ephah of this parched grain and these ten loaves, and carry them quickly to the camp to your brothers;
verses.arminianNotes:
Jesse tells David to take an ephah of parched grain and ten loaves to his brothers at the camp. An ordinary family errand brings David to the battlefield.

Arminian readers note that David goes in simple obedience to his father, and that God works through the free and ordinary choices of people who are faithful in what is in front of them.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that God’s providence often operates through mundane means, so that a father’s errand becomes the route by which the anointed king meets his moment, as Joseph’s errand once led him toward Egypt (Genesis 37:13–14).

Both traditions see ordinary obedience as the setting for God’s extraordinary work.

verses.text: and bring these ten cheeses to the captain of their thousand; and see how your brothers are doing, and bring back news.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Jesse also sends ten cheeses for the commander of the brothers’ unit and asks David to check on his brothers and bring back word. Families supplied soldiers in the field.

Arminian readers note that David is sent to serve and care for others, and that his concern for his brothers’ welfare shows the kind of heart God looks for in a leader.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that David comes as a servant bearing provisions, not as a self-appointed hero, and that God exalts the humble in his own time, a theme that runs through Hannah’s song (2:7–8).

Both traditions see servant-hearted faithfulness in small things as fitting for one who will shepherd God’s people.

verses.text: Now Saul, and they, and all the men of Israel were in the valley of Elah, fighting with the Philistines.
verses.arminianNotes:
Saul and all Israel are in the valley of Elah fighting the Philistines. The narrator restates the military situation as David approaches.

Arminian readers note that the people are formally at war yet have not engaged the champion; outward readiness without trust in God leaves them stalled, which calls readers to examine whether their own activity springs from faith.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the repeated mention of Saul leading the army keeps the rejected king in view, so that the contrast with God’s chosen servant grows sharper as the story moves toward its climax.

Both traditions read the scene as Israel waiting, unknowingly, for the deliverer God is sending.

verses.text: David rose up early in the morning and left the sheep with a keeper, and took the provisions and went, as Jesse had commanded him. He came to the place of the wagons as the army which was going out to the fight shouted for the battle.
verses.arminianNotes:
David rises early, leaves the sheep with a keeper, and arrives as the army goes out to its battle line shouting. He is responsible about both his flock and his errand.

Arminian readers note that David does not abandon the sheep but arranges for their care, showing a conscientious character that God’s grace forms and that David willingly cultivates.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the army’s shouting rings hollow, since no one will actually face the champion, and that true courage will come not from noise but from God’s chosen servant who trusts him.

Both traditions note David’s faithfulness and the emptiness of Israel’s battle cry without faith behind it.

verses.text: Israel and the Philistines put the battle in array, army against army.
verses.arminianNotes:
Israel and the Philistines draw up their lines, army against army. The scene is set for a clash that keeps not happening.

Arminian readers note that the daily ritual of lining up without fighting pictures religious or national activity that has lost its living connection to trust in God, which remains a danger for God’s people in every age.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the formal battle array emphasizes human arrangements, while the decisive act will come from God working through an unarmored shepherd, showing that salvation belongs to the LORD.

Both traditions see the standoff as preparing for a deliverance that human strategy has failed to achieve.

verses.text: David left his baggage in the hand of the keeper of the baggage and ran to the army, and came and greeted his brothers.
verses.arminianNotes:
David leaves his baggage with the keeper, runs to the battle line, and greets his brothers. He is eager and engaged.

Arminian readers note that David’s eagerness to go toward the front, rather than stay with the supplies, reveals a heart already inclined toward God’s cause, though he has come only as a messenger.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that David’s arrival at the line places him exactly where God intends him to be at the moment Goliath appears, an example of the quiet providence that orders even timing and place.

Both traditions see David’s movement toward his brothers as the narrative step that brings him face to face with Israel’s crisis.

verses.text: As he talked with them, behold, the champion, the Philistine of Gath, Goliath by name, came up out of the ranks of the Philistines, and said the same words; and David heard them.
verses.arminianNotes:
As David talks with his brothers, Goliath comes up and repeats his challenge, and David hears it. This is the first time David hears the taunt.

Arminian readers note that hearing the challenge confronts David with a choice; faith becomes visible in how a person responds when God’s honor is publicly despised.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the champion speaks the same words he has spoken for forty days, but now a hearer is present whom God has prepared, so the same challenge meets a different heart.

Both traditions read David’s hearing as the turning point at which the crisis meets faith.

verses.text: All the men of Israel, when they saw the man, fled from him and were terrified.
verses.arminianNotes:
All the men of Israel flee from Goliath in terror when they see him. The army retreats from the mere sight of the champion.

Arminian readers note that fear spreads through the ranks and becomes collective, and that God’s people are responsible to resist such fear by recalling his past deliverances.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the whole army’s flight shows the helplessness of human strength without God, and sets off David’s faith as something God has worked in him rather than a quality shared by the nation at large.

Both traditions see Israel’s panic as the opposite of the trust in the living God that David will display.

verses.text: The men of Israel said, “Have you seen this man who has come up? He has surely come up to defy Israel. The king will give great riches to the man who kills him, and will give him his daughter, and will make his father’s house tax-free in Israel.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The men tell each other that the king will give great riches, his daughter and tax freedom for the man’s family to whoever kills Goliath. The reward sets up later events in chapter 18.

Arminian readers note that the promised reward is a human incentive, yet no one responds to it; the narrative suggests that worldly reward cannot produce true courage.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Saul’s promise of his daughter will later become a tool of his scheming (18:17–27), and that God will overrule even Saul’s manipulations to advance David.

Both traditions observe that David’s motive, voiced in the next verse, rests on God’s honor rather than on Saul’s rewards.

verses.text: David spoke to the men who stood by him, saying, “What shall be done to the man who kills this Philistine and takes away the reproach from Israel? For who is this uncircumcised Philistine, that he should defy the armies of the living God?”
verses.arminianNotes:
David asks what will be done for the man who removes Israel’s reproach, and asks who this uncircumcised Philistine is to defy “the armies of the living God”. His question reframes the conflict.

Arminian readers note that David sees what the others miss: the issue is not military size but covenant relationship, and he responds with faith that God will defend his own honor.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that David calls Goliath uncircumcised, outside the covenant, and names Israel’s God as the living God in contrast to lifeless idols, which grounds his confidence in who God is rather than in his own ability.

Both traditions treat this verse as a theological key to the chapter.

verses.text: The people answered him in this way, saying, “So shall it be done to the man who kills him.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The people answer David by repeating what will be done for the man who kills Goliath. They restate the king’s promise.

Arminian readers note that the people can repeat the terms of reward but not the faith David expresses, showing that knowing about promised blessings is different from trusting God enough to act.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the crowd’s answer focuses on reward while David’s question focused on God’s honor, a contrast that highlights the different heart God has given his chosen servant (16:7, 13).

Both traditions see the exchange as revealing that David’s zeal is for the LORD’s name.

verses.text: Eliab his oldest brother heard when he spoke to the men; and Eliab’s anger burned against David, and he said, “Why have you come down? With whom have you left those few sheep in the wilderness? I know your pride and the evil of your heart; for you have come down that you might see the battle.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Eliab, David’s oldest brother, angrily accuses David of pride and an evil heart, claiming he only came to watch the battle. Eliab misjudges his brother’s motives.

Arminian readers note that the accusation is unjust and may reflect Eliab’s own wounded pride after being passed over, and that believers are warned against attributing bad motives to others without cause.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note the irony that Eliab, whose appearance had impressed Samuel (16:6–7), presumes to read David’s heart, though the LORD alone looks on the heart.

Both traditions read Eliab’s anger as a human obstacle that David must not let deter him from faithful action.

verses.text: David said, “What have I now done? Is there not a cause?”
verses.arminianNotes:
David replies asking what he has done now, and whether there is not a reason. He does not retaliate.

Arminian readers note that David’s restraint shows self-control and focus; he refuses to be drawn into a family quarrel when a greater matter is at stake, a mature response that faith makes possible.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that David’s brief answer turns from personal insult to the cause at hand, and that God’s servants are often misunderstood by those nearest them, as Joseph was and as Jesus was by his own family (Mark 3:21).

Both traditions see David’s response as wise and restrained.

verses.text: He turned away from him toward another, and spoke like that again; and the people answered him again the same way.
verses.arminianNotes:
David turns from Eliab to someone else, asks the same question, and gets the same answer. He keeps pursuing the matter.

Arminian readers note that David persists despite discouragement, and that perseverance in a righteous cause is an expression of faith, not stubbornness, when it is grounded in God’s honor rather than self-promotion.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that David’s persistence moves the story toward Saul, so that God’s appointed means bring his servant into the king’s presence, showing how providence works through determined human action.

Both traditions read his persistence as the step that leads him to volunteer before the king.
